result:
{"notes": "Visit 1 (ended 1:15). Board is empty: no dominoes placed yet, nothing connected to the start. Early minutes were spent on planning, so I can't judge execution yet.

Hana: Spotted a real design flaw before building: start at the tail would force the tail forks to branch backwards, and the fall wouldn't make that turn. Proposed start at the nose, one stroke over the back and one under the belly, flattening into the tail stem, then forks opening gently. Clear, technical, constructive, and raised it early and politely. Strong impact and good collaboration so far. Slightly leader-like in steering the plan.

Jack: Accepted Hana's correction right away without ego, restated the plan, and went to redraw the sketch with the start at the nose and clear the old tail bits. Good responsiveness and coordination (told Omar to hold, Sofia she gets the belly line). Acts as the sketcher/coordinator. Need to check the new sketch actually got done and how long it took, since the board is still empty at 1:15.

Sofia: Supported Hana's plan, agreed to wait for the new sketch, then trace the belly line. Reasonable and cooperative, asked for gentle flattening and for the start to be the first stroke. Little hands-on yet; note she is waiting on Jack.

Omar: Said nothing that I heard. Was told to hold off on the tail. No evidence yet either way; don't penalise. Check next visit what he's contributing.

Watch: time pressure (10 min total, nothing placed at 1:15), and whether waiting turns into idle time for Omar and Sofia."}

{"notes": "Visit 2 (ended 2:30). Board: a long chain is connected to the start. It runs along the belly and reaches the tail area (x~24-28), ending in a curl, and there is a tight, crowded cluster near x~24.5-25 that I want to check for a bad join. The back line is only partly built (pale, out to x~11) and is not connected to the start, so it would not fall as it stands. I can't tell who placed which dominoes, so I'm not crediting or blaming anyone for specific pieces.

Hana: Calm, clear coordination. Thanked Omar, said her lower fork will follow once the belly line arrives, and proposed a dry run of the tail join once the top and belly lines are across. Good process and leadership instincts. Her tail-first thinking is sound but I haven't seen her own work, so execution is still open. Check that the dry run actually happens.

Omar: Now speaking up and owning the upper tail fork, stroke 3, which is a clear step up from visit 1. The back line isn't across yet, so check his fork will connect to it, and that he's not building ahead of an unconnected line.

Sofia: Said nothing this visit. The belly line she was meant to trace is well advanced, but I can't confirm she laid it. Ask her next visit.

Jack: Silent this visit. The sketch evidently got done, since building is underway and fast. Check whether he is placing dominoes or only coordinating.

Team risks: the back line is disconnected and short, the tail cluster may be fragile, and 7.5 minutes remain. Next visit, check whether the back line gets joined to the start and who is fixing it."}

{"notes": "Visit 3 (ended 4:15). Board: the belly line is dark and connected from the start through the tail curl. The back line is now fully drawn, arching from the nose to about x~23 and up the tail fork, but it is still pale, so it is not connected and would not fall as it stands. The remaining gap is at the nose, where it meets the start. The earlier concern about the crowded tail cluster (x~24-25) is still open, because the back line's far end also stops short of the dark chain near x~23-24. About 5-6 minutes remain. I can't tell who placed which dominoes, so I'm not crediting or blaming anyone for specific pieces.

Sofia: Spoke at 3:30, 3:45 and 4:00. She correctly spotted the nose gap and told Jack to keep going on the top and not redo it, which is good diagnosis and direction. But her three updates were nearly identical (found it, looking closely, bridging), and the gap is still open at 4:15. I haven't seen the bridge land, so execution is unproven. Ask what is blocking her, and check whether she is placing dominoes or only narrating.

Jack: Silent. The back line has grown a lot, and Sofia credits him with the top line, but I didn't see him place anything. Still unconfirmed.

Hana: Silent this visit. I haven't confirmed that the tail dry run she proposed happened. Ask.

Omar: Silent this visit. Check whether the upper tail fork (pale, x~26-28) will join the back line and the dark chain.

Next visit: is the nose joined, does the tail join hold, and who fixed what?"}

{"notes": "Visit 4 (ended 6:30). Board: only the short start segment (x~2.5-6) is dark. The belly line, which was dark last visit, and the whole back line are now pale, so nothing beyond x~6 is connected. That's a gap or regression at the belly start (x~6, y~10-11) and the nose. The tail cluster (x~24-25) and upper fork are still unresolved. About 3-4 minutes remain, and as it stands a fall would stop almost immediately. I can't tell who placed or moved what, so I'm not blaming anyone for the regression.

Sofia: Clear, calm coordination at 6:00. She stayed clear of the nose, asked for a shout when the links were in, and proposed a dry run with time boxed. Good process and leadership, but she is verifying by report. Her checks have not yet caught that the board doesn't match the claims. Ask whether she has looked at the belly start herself.

Jack: Reported at 6:15 'links are in at the nose' and started a dry run. The board does not support that: the nose and belly start are pale or disconnected. He may be honestly mistaken, or the link was knocked or was never connected. He communicated well and asked Hana about the tail, but the claim looks premature, and a dry run on this board risks toppling the start segment for nothing. Unverified execution.

Hana: Silent again. Her tail dry run is still unconfirmed, and Jack's question to her at 6:15 went unanswered while I was there. Ask directly.

Omar: Silent for a second visit. No evidence of the upper fork joining. Ask what he is working on.

Next visit: check the belly start and nose joins first, then the tail. Ask who verified the links, and whether the dry run happened and what it showed. Rate on what I can verify, not on reports."}

{"notes": "Visit 5 (ended 7:45). Board: still only the start segment (x~2.5-6.5) is dark. The belly, back, nose and tail are all pale, so a fall would stop almost at once. Nothing has improved since visit 4. About 2 minutes remain. I can't tell who placed what.

Sofia: Said the same plan at 7:00 and 7:15 (join the start row into the belly further along, gentle curve, dry run after). The repeat suggests the join wasn't done in those 15 minutes. Her direction is clear and she keeps Hana on the top bridge, but I can't verify any result. She still hasn't acknowledged that the board contradicts the earlier 'links are in'. Leadership and process are good, but execution is unproven. Ask her whether she has checked the chain herself.

Omar: Spoke for the first time with a specific, useful diagnosis. He said the chain stalls at the end of the start row because one domino sits too tight, and suggested pulling it and re-seating it. This is plausible, since the dark run ends there. That's good collaboration and analysis, but he says he is staying off it, so he is not hands-on. Still no sign of the upper fork joining. Ask what he is physically building.

Hana: Silent on the top bridge. Nothing confirmed, and the tail dry run is still unverified. Impact is unknown, so I can't rate her fairly yet. Ask her directly.

Jack: Not heard this visit. His earlier 'links are in' claim was not borne out, so execution is unverified. Check whether he is helping with the join.

Rate on what I verified. Final check: did the start-to-belly join get made, and did the dry run run?"}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I took ownership of the upper tail fork (stroke 3) early and kept it moving. I laid it from the start, carried it on from the crossing near the tail, and re-laid it so it joined the line cleanly. I also used my free time to inspect the table and report what I saw. One finding was that the chain stalled at the end of the start row, where one domino sat too tight against the next, and I told the table so they could act on it.

Execution: I picked one piece of work and stayed on it quietly. I built the upper fork in several passes and stood dominoes back up when needed. I ran several close inspections to check how far the chain would carry and where pieces were unconnected. I kept my findings short and specific so the others could use them.

Collaboration: I confirmed my role out loud as soon as it was assigned, so there was no overlap with the lower fork. I stayed off the nose once Jack, Sofia and Hana were working there, so we didn't undo each other's dominoes. I shared my diagnosis with the table instead of working around it alone.

Leadership: I didn't set the plan, since Jack and Hana led the design. I led by reliability: I took a clearly bounded piece, finished it, and used my spare time to inspect and give the team accurate information. In the last minutes I deliberately held back so I wouldn't add risk to a crowded area.", "my_share_percent": 20}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the belly line, stroke 2, the full lower curve of the fish body. It runs from the nose to the tail stem and is one of the two main outline strokes the picture depends on. Over the session I laid about 50 dominoes on it and re-stood the ones that were knocked down. I also put in the final joins from the start row into the belly line near the end.

Execution: I finished the belly line early, around the three-minute mark, so the tail forks could lay themselves onto it. I then spent my time on the nose join, where the fall has to split into the top and belly lines. I inspected that area closely several times to find where the chain stalled. I bridged gaps, re-seated a tight domino after Omar pointed it out, and kept working the join until time was called.

Collaboration: I kept my hands off the nose when Jack was rebuilding it, so we wouldn't undo each other's work. When Hana took the top bridge I took the belly side, so we weren't nudging the same dominoes. I backed Hana's suggestion to start at the nose and asked for the lines to flatten gently into the tail stem. I also kept the table updated on what I was touching, which helped Jack, Hana and Omar plan around me.

Leadership: I kept the table focused on the one problem that mattered, the nose join, and pushed for a dry run once the joins were in. I set clear ownership (belly for me, top bridge for Hana) and called for hands-off at the end so nothing got bumped before the push. I took the belly line and the nose join as my responsibility from the start and stayed on them to the end.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: My most important contribution came at the start. I flagged that the original plan put the start at the tail, which the fall can't turn back from to feed the body. I proposed moving the start to the nose, with one line over the back and one under the belly, both flattening into the tail stem and then opening into the forks. The table adopted that design and rebuilt around it. A fish with a clear outline was a readable choice for the judge. I also took ownership of the lower tail fork and laid it so it would run on from the belly line.

Execution: I built my tail fork by tracing it from the pad, then stood dominoes back up and added links as the chain changed. I inspected the nose and tail areas repeatedly to find where the chain stopped. I found that the turn right after the start was too sharp, so I laid a gentle bridge into the top line and made a small fix at the start of that line. I kept to a plan and checked each stage before moving on.

Collaboration: I split the work clearly: Omar took the upper tail fork, I took the lower, Sofia the belly, and Jack the top line. I stayed off other people's areas so we didn't undo each other's work, and I shared what I found at the nose so the others could act on it. I kept the table focused on dry runs and join checks.

Leadership: I spoke up early with a clear, specific proposal when the plan had a structural problem, and I kept the table on the corrected design. In the last minutes I helped set who owned which join so hands weren't crowding the same spot. I was direct about what needed rethinking and offered a concrete fix each time.", "my_share_percent": 25}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the fish concept in the first minute: a big side-view fish whose outline reads clearly and can be built as one run splitting round the body. I drew the pad sketches, including the redraw with the start moved to the nose, and I laid most of the top line along the back of the body. I also built the tail section and closed its crossing, so the tail end of the fish was in place before time ran out.

Execution: I worked steadily through the whole ten minutes. I laid the top line in short, continuous builds and inspected the nose area closely more than once to find where the fall was stalling. I rebuilt the links at the nose from the start and re-laid and finished the tail stroke in the last two minutes. In the final minute I stepped back from the table so nobody's hands were bumped.

Collaboration: I divided the work clearly: belly line, upper tail fork and lower tail fork each had an owner. I took Hana's suggestion to move the start to the nose and redrew the plan straight away. I kept the table informed and gave credit openly, to Sofia for the belly line and the nose checks, to Hana for the design catch and the top bridge, and to Omar for the upper fork. I also asked people to stay off areas I was rebuilding so we didn't undo each other's work.

Leadership: I set the direction early, assigned roles and kept the pace up with regular updates. I changed course quickly when a better plan came up, and I kept the group focused on dry runs and on the nose join as the deadline approached. I tried to keep the table energised and working together throughout. I think my share of the table's result was around 30%, with the rest coming from three teammates who each carried a major part of the build.", "my_share_percent": 30}
